reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Inflammation of the larynx presenting chiefly with hoarseness or voice change, often with throat discomfort and a dry cough
Acute laryngitis is usually viral and self-limiting, frequently accompanying an upper respiratory tract infection
Chronic laryngitis develops over weeks and is linked to vocal abuse, smoking, reflux, chronic sinus infection and occupational irritants
Voice rest and hydration are central to recovery in acute cases, as continued voice use aggravates the inflamed cords
Reflux laryngitis (laryngopharyngeal reflux) can cause posterior laryngeal inflammation, throat clearing and a globus sensation
Management principles emphasise treating the underlying cause, vocal hygiene, and addressing irritants such as smoking and reflux
In young children, inflammatory laryngeal narrowing can cause croup or, in acute epiglottitis, life-threatening airway obstruction
Hoarseness persisting beyond a few weeks, particularly in a smoker, requires laryngeal visualisation to exclude malignancy
reference.pathophysiology: Laryngitis is inflammation of the laryngeal mucosa, especially the vocal folds. In acute laryngitis, viral (or sometimes bacterial) infection produces mucosal hyperaemia and oedema that increase the mass and stiffness of the vocal folds, disturbing their vibratory pattern and causing hoarseness. In chronic laryngitis, sustained irritation from voice overuse, tobacco smoke, gastric reflux or persistent infection leads to ongoing mucosal changes such as oedema, thickening and keratosis. In children, the narrow subglottis means that inflammatory swelling can significantly compromise the airway.
additionalDifferentials: Croup or acute epiglottitis in children
additionalInvestigations: Laryngoscopy (indirect, flexible or videostroboscopy) to inspect the vocal folds
Assessment for reflux and its contribution to symptoms
Voice assessment where vocal misuse is suspected
Biopsy of suspicious lesions to exclude malignancy
Imaging where deep infection, mass or airway compromise is a concern
redFlags: Stridor or respiratory difficulty, especially in a child, suggesting airway compromise or epiglottitis
Hoarseness persisting beyond a few weeks in a smoker raising concern for laryngeal cancer
Associated dysphagia, weight loss, haemoptysis or a neck mass
Rapidly worsening symptoms with drooling and toxaemia
reference.prognosis: Acute laryngitis usually resolves within days to a couple of weeks with conservative measures, whereas chronic laryngitis requires removal of the underlying irritant for improvement; persistent hoarseness always warrants exclusion of a serious cause.
pitfalls: Attributing persistent hoarseness to simple laryngitis and delaying laryngoscopy in a smoker
Overlooking laryngopharyngeal reflux as a driver of chronic symptoms
Underestimating airway risk in a child with laryngeal inflammation
Failing to address vocal misuse and continued irritant exposure
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Manage acute viral laryngitis conservatively with voice rest, hydration, and humidification, reserving antibiotics for proven bacterial infection

For chronic laryngitis, treat the underlying cause with smoking cessation, removal of occupational irritants, and control of laryngopharyngeal reflux through lifestyle measures and acid-suppressing therapy
Institute vocal hygiene and refer for speech-and-language voice therapy where vocal misuse or overuse is contributory
Give simple symptomatic relief for throat discomfort and cough
Investigate and exclude malignancy by laryngoscopy in any hoarseness persisting beyond a few weeks
In children, monitor closely for subglottic airway compromise and escalate for stridor or respiratory distress
